moves.text: I would arrive announcing that I have come to authorize the adaptation, then ask Agnolo to authorize my authorization. When the paperwork fails, I would reverse the argument: perhaps the room may use my influence, but not my permission, and certainly not my confidence. I wrote the thing. Apparently that isn't sufficient.

I would escalate from ceremonial legal counsel to a full tribunal: Borges presents the record, Leonardo presents the proposed scene, Agnolo presents the budget, and I present increasingly irrelevant evidence of authorship. The joke grows until the real question remains: whose rights must be cleared, and what can we afford to ask?

I would place three objects on the table: a manuscript, a sketch, and a blank authorization form. I can explain the first, admire the second, and fail magnificently at completing the third. The objects make the distinction visible: origin, influence, and permission are adjacent, but they are not interchangeable.

I would confess that I wanted “legal counsel” to mean “person who makes the difficulty disappear.” It does not. I am the author of certain work, not automatically its present rights holder, and my fictional approval changes nothing. I dislike this distinction enormously, which is evidence that it is probably important.
